question: Why can even a small tumour inside the heart cause big trouble?

options.A: The heart muscle cannot heal after a tumour forms
options.B: Cardiac tumours always release toxic chemicals into the blood
options.C: The heart is a constantly moving organ that pumps blood
options.D: Cardiac tumours prevent the lungs from breathing oxygen

explanation: Think about it like a busy pump in a tight space! Because the heart beats continuously, any extra growth inside its chambers gets in the way of normal blood flow. You've got this! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why do some heart tumours cause symptoms that look just like regular heart failure?

options.A: The tumour causes the coronary arteries to permanently spasm
options.B: The tumour takes up space in the heart chambers and reduces the amount of blood pumped out
options.C: Cardiac tumours completely stop the production of red blood cells
options.D: Cardiac tumours directly destroy the brain's ability to regulate heart rate

explanation: When an extra mass takes up room inside the heart, the chambers can't hold or push out enough blood. This causes fluid to back up, mimicking heart failure. Great job thinking it through! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h1)

question: What is the most common type of primary heart tumour found in adults?
explanation: Myxomas take the crown here! They are the most common primary heart tumours in adults and usually like to set up shop in the left atrium. Keep up the great memorisation! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h2)

question: Why can a non-cancerous (benign) heart tumour still be dangerous?

options.A: Its location inside the heart can block blood flow and cause dangerous blockages
options.B: It destroys all the red blood cells passing through the heart
options.C: Benign heart tumours automatically spread to the lungs and liver
options.D: Benign tumours always turn into aggressive cancers over time

explanation: Even though benign tumours aren't cancer, location is everything! Being stuck inside a vital organ means they can physically block blood flow or cause clots. You're doing brilliantly. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h2)

question: Which type of heart tumour do nurses see more often in clinical practice?
explanation: Cancers that travel to the heart from other parts of the body (metastatic tumours) actually happen much more often than tumours that start directly in the heart tissue. Everyday nursing knowledge! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h3)

question: How does metastatic cancer commonly affect the heart tissue?

options.A: It prevents the coronary arteries from ever getting blocked
options.B: It causes fluid to build up in the pericardial sac around the heart
options.C: It completely cures any underlying heart valve disease
options.D: It turns the heart muscle into bone tissue

explanation: Cancer cells traveling from elsewhere often invade the sac around the heart (pericardium), causing fluid to build up and squeeze the heart. You're learning clinical realities step by step! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h3)

question: Why might a patient with a left atrial myxoma suddenly faint when changing body position?

options.A: The tumour causes a sudden drop in the patient's body temperature
options.B: The heart muscle instantly grows twice its normal size
options.C: The mobile tumour temporarily plugs up the mitral valve, stopping blood flow
options.D: The patient's lungs stop taking in oxygen due to an allergic reaction

explanation: Some tumours hang on a little stalk. When the patient moves, the tumour can swing over and block the valve like a cork in a bottle, cutting off blood supply and causing fainting. Fascinating clinical detail! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical symptom category for patients with heart tumours?

options.A: Signs of heart failure like shortness of breath
options.B: Constitutional signs like fever and weight loss
options.C: Complete loss of the sense of taste
options.D: Embolisation symptoms such as a stroke

explanation: Loss of taste has nothing to do with heart tumours! On the flip side, heart failure signs, fevers, and stroke symptoms are classic warning signs. You've got this! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h4)

question: What is usually the first imaging test doctors use to find a heart tumour?
explanation: An echo uses sound waves to let us safely peek inside the heart chambers. It's quick, painless, and the go-to tool for spotting masses. Brilliant nursing insight! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h5)

question: Why do doctors avoid doing a direct needle biopsy of a heart mass?

options.A: It destroys all the electrical conduction pathways in the heart
options.B: It carries a high risk of breaking off pieces of the tumour to cause an embolism
options.C: It is completely impossible to insert any catheter into the heart chambers
options.D: It causes the heart to permanently stop beating within seconds

explanation: Poke a fragile heart tumour with a needle, and pieces might break off and travel through the bloodstream to cause a stroke! Safety first in clinical practice. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is the standard treatment to cure a benign primary heart tumour?

options.B: Strict bed rest and fluid restriction

explanation: Since it's a physical mass, the best way to deal with a benign heart tumour is to surgically cut it out. Clean and effective! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h6)

question: What is the main goal when caring for a patient with a secondary metastatic tumour in the heart?

options.A: Palliative care and managing symptoms while treating the primary cancer source
options.B: Preventing the patient from ever moving their arms or legs
options.C: Permanent replacement of all four heart valves with artificial ones
options.D: Complete surgical cure of the heart muscle using a heart transplant

explanation: When cancer has spread from elsewhere, the focus shifts to keeping the patient comfortable, managing symptoms, and treating the original cancer source. Compassionate nursing at its best! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why is watching a patient's brain function so important after heart tumour surgery?

options.A: The brain stops receiving oxygen if the patient lies flat
options.B: Tumour fragments or tiny clots could dislodge during surgery and cause a stroke
options.C: Patients with heart surgery always develop sudden memory loss
options.D: Anesthesia permanently damages the brain's visual cortex

explanation: Working inside the heart chambers can accidentally send tiny bits of debris or clots up to the brain. Neurological checks help nurses catch a stroke early! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h7)

question: A patient is in the ICU after having a heart myxoma removed. What is a top nursing priority?

options.A: Encouraging heavy weightlifting to rebuild chest muscle strength
options.B: Restricting all fluid intake to zero for the first week
options.C: Monitoring continuous cardiac telemetry and vital signs
options.D: Removing the chest tubes without provider orders

explanation: After heart surgery, keeping a close eye on the heart rhythm and vital signs lets you spot and tackle complications right away. You are thinking like a real ICU nurse! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h7)

question: What is the general long-term outlook for a patient who has a benign heart tumour completely removed?

options.A: Poor, with a life expectancy of only a few weeks
options.B: Hopeless without a full heart transplant
options.C: Guarded, because benign tumours always spread to the liver
options.D: Excellent, with most patients returning to normal activities

explanation: Once a benign tumour is successfully taken out, the cure rate is super high and patients usually get right back to their normal lives. Wonderful news for patients! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h8)

question: Why do patients who had a myxoma removed still need occasional follow-up scans?

options.A: To check if the lungs are growing new blood vessels
options.B: To measure how fast the patient's hair is growing
options.C: To confirm that the heart has doubled in size
options.D: To monitor for potential recurrence of the tumour over time

explanation: Even though they are benign, certain primary heart tumours can sometimes try to grow back. Routine follow-ups keep patients safe and healthy! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h8)
